claims.text: Changing equimolar NbMoTaVW to Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 lowers the alloy's valence-electron concentration.
Lowering the VEC in this alloy system will increase ductility.
The ductility increase will arise from greater dislocation mobility caused by a reduced Peierls–Nabarro barrier.
Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 will preserve high modulus and strength relative to equimolar NbMoTaVW.
Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 will have improved work hardening and fracture resistance relative to equimolar NbMoTaVW.
Equimolar NbMoTaVW has a single-phase BCC structure.
Equimolar NbMoTaVW is strong but brittle at room temperature, with approximately 2% compressive fracture strain.
Equimolar NbMoTaVW has a measured compressive yield strength of approximately 1246 MPa.
A computational screen covered 38,326 compositions with elemental concentrations ranging from 2.5 to 40 at.%.
Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 was selected because it combined low VEC with a relatively high predicted Young's modulus.
The modified alloy can be prepared by arc melting under argon.
As-cast Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 maintains a single-phase BCC structure.
As-cast Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 has a dendritic microstructure with an approximately 240 μm grain size.
Reduced VEC promotes intrinsic shear instability and delayed brittle cracking in the retained BCC structure.
Greater dislocation activity facilitates slip, delays brittle fracture, and supports work hardening.
Retention of a relatively high elastic modulus ensures that inherent strength is maintained.
The modified alloy will have substantially greater compressive fracture strain than the approximately 2% baseline, with only modest reductions in yield strength and elastic modulus.
Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 will have lower density than equimolar NbMoTaVW.

The predicted improvements are limited to as-cast Nb–Mo–Ta–V–W alloys tested under room-temperature quasi-static compression and may not persist under different processing histories or phase constitutions.
